say.text: A registrar asks you to elicit the **psoas sign** in a young man with suspected appendicitis. Which manoeuvre do you do?

choices.label: Internal rotation of the flexed right hip
Pressure over the left iliac fossa
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Name the muscle first: the psoas is a hip flexor. Which hip movement puts a flexor on the stretch?
Yes. Extending the right hip stretches the psoas. A **retrocaecal** appendix, the commonest position (K3), lies on that muscle and hurts when it is stretched (K38).
Tempting: both are right-hip manoeuvres, and internal rotation is a real test, so the names blur together.
But that movement stretches a different muscle, the obturator internus (K39). Which hip movement stretches the psoas?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check each name against its muscle: psoas by extension, obturator by internal rotation (K38, K39).

say.text: Tempting: this manoeuvre makes the right iliac fossa hurt, so it feels like the right test for a right-sided sign (K37).
But the psoas sign needs the hip moved, not the abdomen pressed. Which movement do you make for the psoas sign?

sure_note.text: You were sure: pressing the left iliac fossa is Rovsing's sign, which makes the right iliac fossa hurt (K37).

say.text: The psoas sign is **extension of the right hip**: a retrocaecal appendix lying on the psoas hurts when the muscle is stretched (K38).
Internal rotation of the flexed hip is the **obturator** sign, for a pelvic appendix touching obturator internus (K39). Pressure on the left iliac fossa is **Rovsing's** sign (K37).
Your examiner flexes the right hip and rotates the leg inwards. The patient winces with pain. Which sign is this?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Read the movement before the name. Extension of the hip and internal rotation of a flexed hip are different tests. Which one did the examiner do?
Yes. Internal rotation of the flexed hip is the **obturator** sign. It suggests a pelvic appendix touching obturator internus (K39).
Tempting: the psoas sign is the one you just met, and it is also a hip test, so the names blur together.
But the examiner flexed the hip and rotated it inwards. Which sign does that movement give?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin each name to its movement: psoas is extension of the right hip (K38), obturator is internal rotation of the flexed hip (K39).

say.text: Tempting: Rovsing's sign is the test you probably remember best, and it makes right-sided pain (K37).
But no abdominal pressure was applied; the examiner moved the hip. Which sign is named for a hip movement?

sure_note.text: You were sure: Rovsing's sign needs pressure on the left iliac fossa (K37), not a hip movement.

say.text: Name the sign from the movement, not from the last sign you learned.

Internal rotation of the flexed hip: **obturator** sign, pelvic appendix touching obturator internus (K39). Extension of the hip: **psoas** sign, retrocaecal appendix on the psoas (K38). Left iliac fossa pressure: **Rovsing**, right-sided pain (K37).
A young man has right loin pain, pain when you extend his right hip, and little tenderness in front. Which pairing fits?

choices.label: Psoas sign with retrocaecal; obturator sign with pelvic
Psoas sign with pelvic; obturator sign with retrocaecal
Psoas sign with retrocaecal; right rectal tenderness with retrocaecal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Each sign points to one position. Which position does pain on extending the hip point to?
Yes. Pain on hip extension is the psoas sign, pointing to a retrocaecal appendix (K38). The obturator sign points to the pelvic position (K39).
Retrocaecal is the commonest position, and pelvic the second (K3, K93).
Tempting: you have the right two positions, just paired the wrong way round. That slip is easy to make.
But check which position the psoas sign points to. The obturator sign has its own position.

sure_note.text: You were sure: pin each sign to its position. Psoas goes with retrocaecal and obturator with pelvic (K38, K39).

say.text: Tempting: rectal tenderness feels like a serious clue, so it seems to belong with the commonest position.
But the rectal finding points to a different position from the psoas sign. Which position goes with rectal tenderness?

sure_note.text: You were sure: right rectal tenderness suggests a pelvic appendix (K42), not a retrocaecal one.

say.text: Psoas sign: pain on hip extension, from a retrocaecal appendix lying on the psoas (K38). Obturator sign: pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip, from a pelvic appendix (K39).
Right rectal tenderness suggests the pelvic position (K42). Retrocaecal is the commonest and pelvic the second (K3, K93).
Why does a pelvic appendix cause diarrhoea, urinary frequency and right rectal tenderness?

choices.label: It lies on the psoas muscle, which it stretches on hip extension
It lies behind the caecum, irritating the ureter as it passes
It lies against the rectum and bladder, irritating them
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Match each symptom to an organ. Which organ, when irritated, gives diarrhoea, and which gives frequency?
Yes. A pelvic appendix lies against the rectum and bladder, so it irritates them (K34).
That explains the diarrhoea, the frequency and the right-sided rectal tenderness (K34, K42).
Tempting: the psoas sign is the position clue you know best, so the psoas feels like the answer for any appendix.
But a psoas contact gives pain on hip extension, not bladder or rectal symptoms. Which organ does a pelvic appendix touch?

sure_note.text: You were sure: a pelvic appendix touches the rectum and bladder (K34), while the psoas position gives hip-extension pain (K38).

say.text: Tempting: the ureter lies at the back of the abdomen near the caecum, so a retrocaecal appendix seems to reach it.
But a retrocaecal appendix gives loin pain with little tenderness in front (K33). Which symptoms did the stem name?

sure_note.text: You were sure: the stem names bowel and bladder symptoms, which the pelvic position explains (K34).

say.text: A pelvic appendix lies against the rectum and bladder, so it causes diarrhoea, frequency and right rectal tenderness (K34, K42).
The psoas position gives hip-extension pain (K38). Behind the caecum gives loin pain with little tenderness in front (K33).
In the Alvarado (MANTRELS) score, which two items score 2 points each?

choices.label: Migration of pain and rebound tenderness
Right iliac fossa tenderness and rebound tenderness
Right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Only two items carry 2 points. Think about which are local signs at the site, and which one is a blood test.
Yes. Right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis are the only items worth 2 points each (K7, K107).
Tempting: migration and rebound are signs you can name, so they feel like the heavy items.
But weights come from the table, not from how specific a sign feels. Which two items does the table give 2 points?

sure_note.text: You were sure: migration and rebound each score 1, not 2 (K7, K107).

say.text: Tempting: right iliac fossa tenderness is the right first item, so the next sign that feels specific seems to be rebound.
Half right: one of your two 2-point items is correct. Check the second item against the table.

sure_note.text: You were sure: rebound tenderness scores 1, not 2 (K107).

say.text: Only **right iliac fossa tenderness** and **leucocytosis** score 2 each. Every other item scores 1 (K7).
So migration and rebound score 1 each, and the total is out of 10 (K46).
A patient has migration of pain, nausea, right iliac fossa tenderness, rebound tenderness and leucocytosis. Everything else is normal. What is the Alvarado total?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the two items worth 2 points, then add 1 point for each other item that is present.
Yes. Migration 1, nausea 1, right iliac fossa tenderness 2, rebound 1, leucocytosis 2: that is 7 (K7, K107).
A score of 7 or more makes appendicitis likely (K47).
Tempting: migration and rebound are both real signs, so they feel like they deserve the heavier score.
But only two items score 2. Recount from the table: which items score 2 here?

sure_note.text: You were sure: migration and rebound each score 1, so the total is 7 (K7).

say.text: Tempting: leucocytosis is a blood test, so it feels like a lesser item that scores one point.
But leucocytosis is one of the two 2-point items. Recount the total with that in mind.

sure_note.text: You were sure: leucocytosis scores 2 (K7, K107).

say.text: Migration 1, nausea 1, right iliac fossa tenderness 2, rebound 1, leucocytosis 2: total 7 (K7).
Seven or more makes appendicitis likely (K47).
A young woman has sudden right iliac fossa pain at mid-cycle. There is no migration, she is afebrile, her count is normal, and the pain settles over hours. Most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask two things: what in this stem argues against appendicitis, and what does mid-cycle pain in a woman usually mean?
Yes. Mid-cycle pain from a ruptured Graafian follicle is **mittelschmerz** (K59).
It settles over hours, with no migration, fever or raised count. Right-sided pain is not appendicitis by default.
Tempting: right iliac fossa pain is the classic appendicitis picture, so right-sided pain in a young woman feels like it.
But look at the course: the pain settles and the count is normal. What else gives mid-cycle pain in women?

sure_note.text: You were sure: right iliac fossa pain does not settle the diagnosis by itself (K58, K59).

say.text: A real differential in women (K59), so not a careless pick.
But mid-cycle pain that settles over hours fits mittelschmerz better than a pelvic infection.
Right iliac fossa pain has many causes. In a woman, ectopic pregnancy, ruptured ovarian cyst, pelvic inflammatory disease and mittelschmerz all mimic appendicitis (K59).
Mittelschmerz is the one that settles: a ruptured Graafian follicle (K59). In children, mesenteric lymphadenitis; in adults, ureteric colic and caecal diverticulitis (K58, K60).
